claim: The distributed traffic signal system operates through an emergent consensus mechanism where intersections negotiate timing parameters through iterative message passing to achieve system-wide coherence
mechanism: Each intersection maintains multiple candidate timing parameters and evaluates them based on local metrics. It then shares these candidates with neighbors, which in turn evaluate them based on their local context. Through iterative rounds of evaluation and sharing, the system converges to a consensus set of parameters that represents a balance between local efficiency and global coherence. This mimics the consensus-building behavior observed in slime mold network formation.
evidence: Consensus algorithms are well-established in distributed computing
Emergent consensus is observed in biological systems like slime molds
Multi-agent consensus has been applied to traffic systems with some success
assumptions: Intersections can effectively evaluate and compare multiple timing options
Message passing between intersections can be implemented with low overhead
The consensus process will converge within acceptable timeframes
Local evaluations can adequately represent global traffic conditions
expected_failure_modes: Failure to reach consensus in heterogeneous network conditions
Excessive computational overhead from message passing
Vulnerability to manipulation by malicious intersections
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis applies emergent consensus principles to traffic signal optimization, where intersections collectively determine optimal timing through iterative negotiation rather than individual optimization
testability: The hypothesis can be tested by implementing the consensus mechanism and measuring the quality of the consensus solution, convergence time, and system performance
falsifier: If the system fails to reach a consistent consensus across all intersections or if the consensus solution performs worse than the current fixed-timing system
